speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on Sunday, May 14, close to 10,000 Islanders marched together to protest the Government's decision to close CFB Summerside. Never before in the recent history of our province have so many demonstrated so strongly for something so important to Prince Edward Island. I ask this Government to re-evaluate the decision to close CFB Summerside, and I demand that they think about the many people the closure will affect. The economic impact, as everyone is now aware, would be devastating, but the social impact would be tragic. There would be a loss of community, a loss of confidence to Summerside and its surrounding areas. Although we may not be able to put a dollar figure on these losses, Mr. Speaker, their impacts are very real, and this Government has provided no thought to the people who will suffer as a result of the base closure.

subsubtopic: SUPPLY BILL HELD UP BY SENATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let's face it, democracy in Canada is not faring very well during this Session of Parliament.
First, the Government spent $300 on behalf of every Canadian citizen through the use of Governor General Warrants without the knowledge or consent of Members of the House of Commons. This is a form of theft, and an affront to our Constitution and to hundreds of years of parliamentary tradition and fundamental democratic principles.
When the Government finally did the right thing and asked elected Members of Parliament for the supply of funds, again our democratic process found itself at risk. This time not by the Government, but by the unelected, unaccountable Members of the Senate who stopped the Supply Bill and held up cheques being processed for our war veterans and members of the RCMP. Of course, the Senators' cheques were never in jeopardy.
Does the Senate have the right to initiate money Bills? Clearly not. Should it have the right to hold up, amend, or in any way monkey around with money Bills? Again, absolutely not.
It's high time that this undemocratic, unelected group of Senatorial hacks, flacks, and bagmen resign, or better yet, that we simply abolish this outdated institution called the Senate.

Mr. Speaker, I want to talk briefly on the topic of employment equity. If our nation is to achieve its full potential, we must offer equal opportunities to all.
At the same time, we must respect the rights of individuals. People must be given the choice to make their own decisions, whether it be for career, family, or a combination of both.
Through the Employment Equity Act the federal Government is giving more opportunities to those people who choose to work and who traditionally have been at a disadvantage.
All Canadians deserve the opportunity to choose what they want to do with their lives. Everyone, male or female, should have the opportunity to make their own choices regarding career and family.
As Parliamentarians, through legislation and example, we must ensure that all Canadians are given equal opportunities.

Mr. Speaker, today is World Telecommunications Day. One hundred and sixty-five countries celebrate co-operation in developing a world-wide telecommunications system that includes, in part, local and long-distance telephone networks and international telephone links. At the same time, the Department of Communications celebrates 20 years of work on Canadian communications and cultural endeavours.
Europe is developing a more unified system for 1992, and Japan and the United States are moving ahead. The time has come to establish a modem Canadian national telecommunications policy; this is vital to all parts of this vast country. I call on the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) to join and support this effort. These issues affect every business, every household, and every individual who uses a phone or receives digital information.
Let us look ahead and address the challenges to maximize benefits from this information age. Let us hear what Canadians think about long-distance competition, about how their phones and data services should work, and what our regulations should be in this era of rapid technological change.

May 17, 1989

The shape of our future for the 21st Century as a vibrant nation depends on an affordable, accessible, modem, flexible communication policy that benefits all Canadians in all regions.

Mr. Speaker, the frustration that Canadians have felt over the case of Charles Ng cannot even begin to compare with the pain and suffering the families of the alleged victims have had to endure, as they have been forced to live over and over the horrible nightmare of the deaths of their loved ones. Some of those American families are present in the House today.
As time marches on, and as a fugitive plays out seven possible court appearances, the ability of foreign authorities to properly dispense justice becomes increasingly difficult. While fugitives such as Charles Ng are allowed to remain in this country, and as witnesses die or move away, the ability to obtain convictions in court continues to slip away. Does Canada really want to become an accessory to a possible miscarriage of justice? Are we turning Canada into a haven for American killers attempting to escape justice in their own country?
I urge the Government of Canada to move quickly with changes to the Extradition Act, and should it see fit, support my private Member's Bill C-209.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Tbraer (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF CUTS TO WESTERN CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Conservatives are beginning to shut down the regions of our country.
In the last 24 hours we have learned that the Government is not content with savaging the economy of Atlantic Canada, it is now beginning to ravage the economy of western Canada. We have learned that the Port of Churchill, Manitoba, will be shut down for grain
shipments. We have learned that the federal Government is slashing the $420-million worth of forestry development agreements. This morning we learned that spending by the Western Economic Diversification Agency is being cut by $55 million per year.
How can the Prime Minister justify those actions, all of which will prove devastating to western Canada?

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF CUTS TO WESTERN CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, regional development expenditure in western Canada in the five-year period from 1979 to 1984 averaged $160 million a year. In the past five-year period from 1984 to this year, that has increased to $196 million per year. Over the next five-year period it will increase to $363 million a year. That is an increase of 85 per cent. That is why there is such strong regional development in western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, western diversification cut. Regional development agreements cut. Forestry agreements cut. Ports closed. Armed Forces bases closed. VIA Rail cut. Freight rates increased. Crop insurance cut. Drought assistance late. Branch line rehabilitation cut. New value-added tax on agricultural inputs. Special grains programs cut. Cash advances for grain storage cut. Rural post offices closed. Initial crop prices down.
The Conservatives have adopted a scorched-earth policy for western Canada.
I want to ask the Prime Minister why, by these actions, is he forcing young people to leave the land in western Canada? Why is he forcing the abandonment of western Canadian communities?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Corbeil (Minister of Labour) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-8, an Act to amend the Department of Labour Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank you and all Hon. Members for giving me this opportunity to introduce a short amendment to the Department of Labour Act.
This amendment is necessary to enable my Department to continue to assist older employees who have been affected by a permanent reduction in the work force and who, after making every attempt to find other employment and exhausting their entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits, still have no prospects of re-entering the labour market.
The ongoing adjustment of employees is a basic component of the economic adjustment process in Canada. For instance, since the turn of the century we have experienced a major shift of employment from the primary and manufacturing sectors to the service industries. The latter now employ 71 per cent of Canadian workers, compared with 32 per cent at the beginning of this century.
The industries themselves have experienced considerable changes as well. For every ten manufacturing companies that were operational in 1971, only six were still operational in 1980. Four closed down but, on the other hand five new companies were formed during the same period, for every group of ten.
Mr. Speaker, every year, four million workers, which is one-third of the labour force, change jobs in Canada.
Labour
Mr. Speaker, these changes are both healthy and necessary to maintain a strong and viable economy. They are also an indication of the flexibility, open attitude and adaptability of Canada's labour force.
However, one group of workers is facing some very specific adjustment problems. I am referring to those who are suddenly deprived of their jobs after reaching the age of 55. Their problems are aggravated by the competition they get from an educated and competent baby-boom generation that is flooding the labour market.
As a result, many of those Canadians to whom our country owes so much have been brutally uprooted from a job environment to which they have often dedicated their entire working lives. These people are now more or less on the street, because new technology has made their skills and capabilities obsolete.
The increasing number of people in this situation on the labour market makes it even harder to arrange for rehiring of individuals in similar jobs.

The challenge of facilitating labour market adjustment for laid-off older workers is most important as we are dealing with Canada's most loyal and experienced employees. I would like to focus briefly on some of the problems faced by these older workers.
The unemployment rate is the most visible indicator of the effects of adjustment. Traditionally, unemployment rates are lowest for the older age group. This remains true today, but the gap has narrowed since the employment peak of 1981 when workers aged 55 to 64 experienced an unemployment rate of only 4.4 per cent, or just above half of the national rate. The unemployment rate for older workers has increased to 6.2 per cent, or to just over three-quarters of the national rate.

A recent Statistics Canada study of laid-off workers highlighted some special problems of a growing number of unemployed older workers. It was observed that laid-off older workers are unemployed longer than younger workers. The study showed that 40 per cent of these laid-off older workers were jobless for over six

May 17, 1989
Labour
months, compared to 25 per cent for the 25-44 age group.
It was also found, Mr. Speaker, that older workers are more likely to get discouraged after looking for a job for a long time and to withdraw from the labour market. Forty-two per cent of these permanently laid-off workers do not find a job and simply give up.
The tendency of older workers to get discouraged and withdraw from the labour market contributes to lowering the participation rate for this age group. Only half of those aged 55 to 64 are in the labour force, compared to about 80 per cent for the 25-54 age group.
Permanently laid-off older workers who find another job accept a 12 per cent salary decrease, on average.
That is the largest drop for all age groups, Mr. Speaker.
Inadequate retraining and lack of mobility for older workers add to their difficulties. In fact, the Statistics Canada study showed that the retraining rate for laid-off older workers is one third of what it is for the others. Only 6 per cent of laid-off workers 55 and over register for any retraining course, compared to 18 per cent for those under 55.
-
The study also revealed that, proportionately, twice as many workers who were under 55 when they were laid off permanently during the 1981-82 recession found another job. Eighteen per cent of those under 55 went back to work, compared to six per cent of those 55 and older. We all understand, I am sure, how difficult it must be for these workers to suddenly break the ties forged over a lifetime with companions who have shared their joys, happiness, sorrows and dedication.
As Hon. Members from all parties know, for many years Labour Canada has actively assisted some of these laid-off older workers. In fact, at the present time, nearly 8,000 of these workers are receiving assistance under the Labour Adjustment Benefits Act, commonly known as the LAB Program.
I immediately wish to reassure the House, Mr. Speaker, that the brief amendment we are considering today will in no way harm these beneficiaries. They will
continue to receive the full amount of their present LAB benefits until they reach age 65.

The LAB Program, however, has a number of serious flaws. First, the only industries designated nationally for assistance were the very narrow group of textile, clothing, footwear and tanning industries. Second, the LAB Program contains very poor work incentives because, even before taking income tax into account, 60 per cent of every dollar earned by beneficiaries is lost through reduced benefits. Third, it discourages private-sector involvement by fully deducting from LAB payments all benefits offered by employers. Fourth, it offers no opportunities for the provinces to participate in helping older workers.
For these reasons, in 1985 and 1986 we undertook full consultation with the provinces, business, and unions on the need for improved assistance for laid off older workers. They encouraged us to find a better way to help those workers.
This led the federal Government in its 1986 Budget to indicate its intention to work with the provinces to develop a new program for older-worker adjustment, and to commit $125 million to the program.
Two and a half years of very constructive discussions with the provinces, and more than 35 federal-provincial Ministerial meetings, led to the joint development of the new program for older-worker adjustment, the POWA Program, as it is commonly known.
Details of an implementation plan for POWA were announced on October 6, 1988. Eight provinces, namely, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta have already agreed to participate in POWA. This is an outstanding degree of initial provincial participation for a new cost-shared federal-provincial program, and a significant accomplishment.
For example, the hospital insurance plan was launched in 1958 with five participating provinces. It took until 1961 for all provinces and territories to participate. Although the Medicare system was adopted in 1966, only two provinces were participating in the program by 1968. It took until 1972, six full years later, for all provinces and territories to join.

With regard to Ontario and British Columbia, which have not yet agreed to participate in POWA, our continuing discussions regarding their participation in the new program are encouraging.

The basic principles of POWA, which are incorporated in the proposed legislation before the House today, are as follows: First, POWA applies to all sectors and all regions; second, it is based on full partnership with the provinces; third, it gives the employer a chance to participate; and fourth, it provides better incentives for going back to work.
Hon. Members will note that these principles are fairer than those of LAB, its predecessor. The proposed change in the legislation, Mr. Speaker, also includes appropriate transitional measures for older workers in sectors formerly targeted by LAB.
In the case of industries that were targeted by LAB in August 1986, when most of the designations expired, the proposed amendment guarantees that termination of employment that took place between the date of expiry of these designations and January 1, 1988, the date on which POWA came into effect, may be considered for the purposes of the new program. In all cases of termination of employment considered under POWA and which occurred between August 1986 and October 6, 1988, when POWA was announced, the proposed amendment will make it possible to consider as well workers below the age of 55 whose age plus number of years of service equals 80 or more, because their situation would normally have been considered under LAB. These transitional measures are necessary to provide for a reasonable continuity between LAB and POWA in the case of workers in industries formerly designated under LAB.
Since the POWA implementation plan was announced on October 6, 1988, we and our provincial partners have received requests to consider hundreds of terminations of employment.

Speedy passage of this amendment would enable us to more promptly assist some of the laid off older workers who have already exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits. Those workers have pressing needs. Organizations such as the Canadian Labour Market and Productivity Centre, the Advisory Council on Adjustment, the Economic Council of Canada, and the Canada

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today in the debate on second reading of Bill C-8, an Act to amend the Department of Labour Act. It is a relief for me, and indeed for all the people of Canada who may benefit from this legislation, to finally see a Bill in the House. We have been awaiting introduction of this Bill for nearly three years. We have been awaiting the results of a promise that the Government made to initiate a program of income-support and retraining for older workers.
Some older workers were and in fact still are having difficulty finding employment after losing their jobs. Those difficulties have been well documented. The report on Human Rights and Ageing in Canada tabled in the House of Commons on August 16,1986 noted a rapid increase in the number of Canadians aged 45 to 65. Aging workers have a harder time finding employment, and lengthy periods of unemployment exist for older workers.
The committee recommended, among other things, that the Government should designate older workers as target groups for job strategies; that the Government should explore the impact of corporation rationalization, plant closures, and corporate take-overs on older workers. That was in August, 1986. Since then various interest groups have spoken out on the perils of older workers in Canada. More recently the Government's de Grandpre report recommended that all provinces and territories participate in the Program for Older Worker Adjustment. That is exactly what this Bill represents, but the report also concluded that the Program for Older Worker Adjustment, or POWA as it is known, provides assistance only to those older workers involved in major

It is the responsibility of the Government, in conjunction with the Minister of Labour and his Department, to pursue other avenues of assistance to older workers. This is especially important for older individual workers who do not fall under the mandate of POWA and for older workers who are employed by small companies.
On November 22, 1984, the Minister of Employment and Immigration requested that the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council undertake a study of the problems faced by older workers in Canada, older workers who are unemployed as a result of economic and technological changes that took place in Canada at that time.
Included in the mandate was the examination of the adequacy of current measures to assist older workers and, if necessary, to submit possible recommendations to the problem.
The council noted that the Canadian labour force and the general population was aging. The proportion of persons in the age 45 to 64 group was also growing at a tremendous rate.
The council estimated that there were 4.9 million people in the age groups, 2.4 million of these people were male and 2.5 million were female. They further estimate that there would be 6.7 million in the age group, consisting of 3.3 million male and 3.4 million female workers, by the year 2001. That date that seemed so far away five years ago is now just around the comer.
It is important to note that older workers have a significant characteristic. They remain unemployed longer than workers in other age groups. Even more startling is that over the past 10 to 15 years there has been a decline in labour force participation by older workers, particularly men in the 55 to 64 age bracket.
In a special study conducted by Statistics Canada in January, 1968, to gather information on labour market adjustment experiences, the survey highlighted marked differences between older workers and their counterparts between the ages of 25 and 54.
The study noted that older workers who lost their job experienced much greater labour market adjustment difficulties than younger workers. As of January, 1986, only 39 per cent of older workers who lost their jobs between the 1981 to 1984 period were employed, in comparison with 65 per cent of the 25 to 54 year old group which had obtained employment. In addition, about 41 per cent of the older workers had left the labour force while only 14 per cent of the younger workers had done so. Even the older workers who did find employment took an average of 37 weeks to do so. This represented a period of 10 weeks longer than younger workers.
These are startling statistics. But there is more. Older workers who managed to find a new job suffered a larger loss in remuneration than younger job losers. In essence, remunerations were 12 per cent lower for older workers compared to 2 per cent for younger workers.
When one compares labour force participation in the provinces, it is interesting that in Ontario, the prairie provinces and British Columbia, participation by 55 to 65 year old Canadians was high as of 1986. More than half were in the labour force. In Quebec and the Atlantic provinces, the corresponding figure was around 40 per cent.
When older workers are displaced from traditional industries, there is no guarantee that they will easily find suitable employment. This is because of the fact that most new jobs today are in the service sector and these jobs are not comparable in terms of wages. As previously mentioned, displaced older workers who manage to find employment do so at substantially reduced wages.
Education is also a factor for older workers. It can be detrimental. On the average, older workers possess fewer years of formal education. Given this reality, they are at a disadvantage when competing against younger workers in the labour market. Characteristics such as loyalty, conscientiousness and lower rates of turnover are more often than not ignored.
Another misconception is that older workers are resistant to change. According to the research conducted by the Labour Council of Metropolitan Toronto, it was noted that:

I would like now to deal with some other aspects of this legislation. When considering this legislation, one must keep in mind the fact that the present federal Government did not develop the concept of programs to assist the older worker. Therefore, Canadians should not be overly pleased to see legislation tabled almost three years after it was promised by the Government, legislation in the form of a relief package that has many weaknesses. It has so many weaknesses that if they are not watched closely, they may prove to be more detrimental than beneficial.
Canada's older workers are being squeezed out of their jobs, and thus their place in society. This program offers no more in the way of financial assistance to the these Canadians than what existed in the Labour Adjustment Benefit Program which spent $125.6 million from 1983-84 to 1985-86. It is important to note that this program was founded by the Liberal Government in the 1970s.
It must also be remembered that in its February, 1986 Budget the Government cancelled the LAB program and it is only now that we have a new program to assist these older workers.
Currently, at the federal level there are no labour market adjustment programs specifically targeted to older workers. This proposed program for older worker adjustment being discussed today is an income maintenance program.
Income maintenance to older laid-off employees is not a new idea. The Liberal Government initiated the Adjustments Assistance Benefits Program in 1972. Labour Canada developed this program to ease the burden for older employees who were laid off as a result of less restrictive import quotas being introduced into the textile and clothing industries. The program was also in response to the introduction of modernization programs initiated to improve the ability of these industries to compete with competitive imports.
The Adjustment Assistance Benefits Program was further expanded in 1978 as a result of restructuring in the footwear and tanning industries. This came about as a consequence of the then Government's footwear and tanning industry sector strategy.

These programs provided benefits to qualified individuals aged 54 and older who had been employed as production workers in the industry for at least 10 of the 15 years preceding lay-off.
Later in the decade all adjustment measures available to industry and labour were reviewed and special adjustment initiatives were created to respond to the more competitive activity in the industries within Canada. The Labour Adjustments Benefits Program was thus established. In 1982, by virtue of the Labour Adjustment Benefit Act, these Adjustment Assistance Benefits Programs were consolidated. As mentioned earlier, the Government cancelled these programs in February, 1986, and the older workers in Canada have had no assistance programs since then.
I am pleased to see that these workers who fell into the cracks between August 12, 1986 and today will be taken care of with this legislation. It was almost a three year wait, but this typifies the present Government. It has a history of promises that have either never been kept or, if they do come through, there is usually an exorbitant waiting period attached to the promise.
I am quite aware that government Members will argue that Bill C-8, the Program for Older Worker Adjustment, is a program not limited to designated industries as is the Labour Adjustment Benefits Program. They will argue that POWA will cover lay-offs from all private sector industries and commercial Crown corporations. They will say that POWA will assist individuals subject to unemployment as part of a major permanent lay-off and that these lay-offs will be assessed individually taking into account a full range of relevant considerations.
These considerations are to include significant economic disruption in the region, major loss of employment in the industry, lay-offs very large relative to the size of the community, a large proportion of older workers affected, permanent losses of jobs, absence of alternative economic opportunities, no prospects for re-employment of laid-off older workers and no realistic possibility that retraining or mobility will lead to job opportunities.
This does not take into account the older workers who fall through the cracks of POWA. They could include individuals who are not retrainable for a variety of reasons. They could also include any older workers who are not part of major permanent lay-offs. What is a

Labour
major lay-off? Do we go by numbers of employees in a region or do we judge the severity according to an individual's circumstances?
Under the former Labour Adjustment Benefits Program, keeping in mind it covered designated industries, the criteria for eligibility was the following:
The number of employees in the establishment must have been reduced as a result of lay-offs, in any 12-month period including the employee's effective date of lay-off by at least 10 per cent or 50 employees, whichever is less.
Once again, what will constitute, in the minds of federal and provincial Governments, a major permanent lay-off? Take, for example a shoe repairman who has been working at the same firm for 35 years. Suddenly the firm goes bankrupt, closes down and he is unemployed. This is a major lay-off for this individual. Will it be a major lay-off under POWA?
The Canadian Labour Congress, in its presentation to the Liberal task force on trade's public forum on adjustment hearing held February 7, 1989, noted that unemployment should be accepted only as a last resort. To this end, the CLC made several recommendations, including the cancellation of the program for older workers and its replacement with a credible program for older workers, Government commitment to full employment, one year advance notice of plant closures required of employers employing more than 15 workers and six months advance notice of plant closures required of firms with fewer than 15 employees.
In addition, the Canadian Labour Market Productivity Centre made a variety of recommendations at the above-mentioned hearings. These included the creation of a nation-wide program for older worker adjustments. As well, the CSN argued that the program for older workers was ineffective and in need of a complete overhaul. They did, however, call for more federal-provincial collaboration in the implementation of adjustment programs in order to remove some of the jurisdictional disputes that arise from their implementation.
To sum up the hearings with respect to older workers, there was a consensus that existing Government programs, particularly the Canadian Jobs Strategy and the Program for Older Workers Adjustment, are inadequate
to meet the difficulties facing Canadians who must deal with the prospect of unemployment.
There is another issue that I believe needs to be addressed given the free trade legislation recently passed and the recent mergers and acquisitions which have occurred. What in this legislation prevents any business or corporation from intentionally down-sizing to eliminate not only older workers but their pensions and benefits as well? What is stopping a company from laying off employees between the ages of 50 and 54 and hiring younger and better educated individuals at lower salaries after a short period of time?
Government Members will answer these questions by saying that this legislation is for major lay-offs from a permanent reduction. That is, the company or business will never return to its former level of employment. I believe that business could exploit this program. This is certainly a possibility, given the sweeping economic changes that our country is facing in light of the free trade legislation. Even prior to free trade, it is a known fact that companies would hire management consultants to re-evaluate their companies employees, bringing about slashes to the average workers just prior to their benefits or pensions kicking in.
With respect to the federal-provincial partnership in this new program, I am quite concerned about the claim that eight out ten provinces have supposedly agreed to participate in the program. The two that are presently not in the fold are Ontario and British Columbia. My home province of Prince Edward Island is listed as one of the eight participating in the program, but I would question what degree this participation entails. I have been informed that P.E.I. has only agreed to participate on a project-by-project basis.
I firmly believe that these supposed levels of participation have to be examined in more detail. Presently, we have no idea what each province has agreed to. We only know that it is a 70 per cent federal and 30 per cent provincial financial split.
This federal-provincial participation begs another question. Why is the federal Government foisting the responsibility of older worker assistance programs on to the provincial Governments? It seems to me that most of the major causes of recent unemployment in Canada are the result of federal initiatives. Why then are the provinces obligated to pay? Maybe this is why some
May 17, 1989

provinces have not agreed to participate and why others are only partially in agreement. These are questions that need to be addressed and we should have answers to them.
This also sets a dangerous precedent. Once the federal-provincial agreements with respect to labour adjustment programs are established, it will be very difficult in the future for provinces to refuse any financial responsibility with respect to similar programs.
Just what provinces will most benefit from such a program given the parameters required for eligibility? Once again, the parameters are major permanent layoffs in private sector industries and commercial Crown corporations, and they must cause real hardship for substantial numbers of older workers.
Given that the principal target groups will be large-scale lay-offs that have a pronounced effect on local communities, it is safe to assume that the majority of the federal allocation of $125 million will go to high density areas, leaving little for the poorer regions that may need it more. What will be the 70 per cent contribution of federal moneys to an area such as Port Hood, Nova Scotia?
The help that this Government says the program will give is only marginal at best for it does little in the way of retraining those nearly retired workers who may still have the aptitude and interest to continue working in areas of their choice.
In conclusion, my colleagues and I in the Liberal Party support the concept of a Bill for older workers, but only if it provides more assistance than the defunct LAB program. There are many areas of concern in this legislation, and unless these are rectified, the Government will once again prove to Canadians that it is unsympathetic to the problems faced by older Canadians who are seeking employment. There must be more done to assist workers, and older workers in particular, who have been displaced by economic adjustments. The Government must be proactive and the Liberal Party will be monitoring its progress in this area.

Mr. Speaker, finally we are getting legislation to help older workers who lose their jobs, but unfortunately this legislation is far from adequate. I will explain that in greater detail in a few minutes.
I said "finally we are getting legislation to help older workers" because it was more than three years ago that the Government announced this program. The Minister of Finance, in making his budget address in February 1986, announced that he was abolishing the Labour Adjustment Benefits Program. He was to replace it with a wonderful new program called "Program for Older Worker Adjustment".
Months went by in 1986, and we did not see this wonderful new program. Opposition members started to rise and ask questions on where the program was. We received no adequate answers. There was delay upon delay. Then 1986 passed, 1987 passed and 1988 passed, but once the election was under way, on October 6,1988 finally the Government announced the program again with a few more details. However there was still no legislation of course; we were in the middle of the election campaign.
If the Government did not have this older worker adjustment program ready on that occasion, it should have kept the old Labour Adjustment Benefits Program in place until the new program was ready. No, it did not do that. It abolished the old program immediately with the Budget of February 1986. It has been some three and a half years and we still do not have the legislation, but at least we have started to debate it. We have gone all this time since February, 1986 with no program whatsoever.
Any reasonable Government would have kept the old program in place, a program which did help older workers when they were laid off permanently. It was not as complete as it should have been. It was not as perfect as it should have been, but at least it was a program that helped older workers who were laid off from work on a permanent basis. The Government abolished that program and promised a new one. As a matter of fact, it gave the impression in the Budget that the new program was going to come on in a matter of weeks, and here we are in 1989 finally debating this new program.
This situation has been allowed to carry on where, the situation where for more than three years we have gone without any program for older worker assistance, despite several reports to the Government pointing out how serious the situation was.
I refer first to a report prepared by the Canadian Employment and Immigration Advisory Council. This council was set up by the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Its report entitled "Older Workers, an Imminent Crisis in the Labour Market" was published in August 1985. In part it read:
There are now more than 300,000 workers between the ages of 45 and 64 officially and unofficially unemployed in Canada. The unemployment rate for this age group increased significantly after 1981, and then took a major jump early in 1985 at a time when unemployment among other age groups decreased or remained stable. Furthermore older workers stay unemployed longer than their younger counterparts.
This report of the advisory council to the Minister of Employment and Immigration contained 10 recommendations on what should be done for older workers in this country, but the Government did not act on any of them.
We also had a report published by Statistics Canada in November 1987 entitled "Older Workers in the Canadian Labour Market". As a result of a special statistics study, this report pointed out: "Results from the 1986 Census show a rapidly aging Canadian population. This trend has its roots in rising life expectancy, low birth rates and the maturing of the post-war baby boom generation. In 1976 Canadians 55 years or more comprised about 17 per cent of the total population. By 1986, 10 years later, the proportion had risen to about 20 per cent, and by the turn of the century this age group could account for nearly one in four Canadians". That would be 25 per cent.
The report went on to point out that, in 1986, four years after the recession, unemployment among older workers was worse than it had been during the depths of the recession in 1982. The unemployment rate for those older workers had risen from 6.9 per cent in 1982 to 7.3 per cent in 1986.
A moment ago I referred to the report published by the Advisory Council. It published a follow-up report on June 22, 1988, one year ago. In publishing this follow-up report on older workers it stated: "It is evident that the unemployment situation of older workers has not improved since 1985 when the Advisory Council report on
May 17, 1989

older workers was published and, in fact, it has deteriorated". From the report in 1985 to last year in June there has been a deterioration of the situation for older workers.
There have been other reports to which the Government should have been paying attention, but it was not. There is a very complete report on older workers by Gladys Dunn. She prepared a report for the Department of Employment and Immigration. She was an individual appointed by the Department to study this problem. Her report was published in 1985.
Among other things, she pointed out that it is a myth that older workers, meaning workers 45 and older, and in some cases it is defined as 55 and older, are unable or are very slow to learn or to be trained. She demonstrated that that was a myth. She also demonstrated that it is a myth that there is declining mental and physical capacity with age. She proved and showed that there are many things that older workers in that age category can do, and can do better than younger people.
The third myth is that older workers are less productive. Again, that is a myth. Older workers are not less productive. The fourth myth she demonstrated was that older workers have more on-the-job accidents. They do not have more on-the-job accidents. The fifth myth was that older workers are absent more often. Again, that was shown in her report not to be true.
In the last Parliament in 1987-88 the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, of which I was a member and which has representatives of all Parties in the House, conducted a review of the Canadian Jobs Strategy. It referred to the problem of older workers. In Recommendation 2.7.8 it stated that older workers be identified as a target group under the Canadian Jobs Strategy. Despite the fact that that was a unanimous recommendation of the Standing Committee, it was not implemented.
Another Standing Committee of the House, the Standing Committee on Human Rights, again a committee representing all Parties of the House, put out a unanimous report on human rights and aging in Canada. Among its recommendations was that Employment and
Labour
Immigration Canada designate older workers, especially those older worker groups prone to long-term unemployment, as a target group for the purposes of the Canadian Jobs Strategy. That was not done either.
There have been many reports and studies that indicated that action was necessary and was essential, but nothing was done for more than three years except another announcement in the middle of the last election campaign.
I have here a report by the Economic Council of Canada entitled: "Managing Adjustment". It also stated that special programs must be implemented for older workers.
I have stories from all over the country which have been reported in the press. In The Hamilton Spectator in August, 1988 there as a story entitled: "Unemployed older workers. Bad enough to lose a job held for years, but governments have done little to help". In the Winnipeg Free Press in August, 1988 there was an article entitled: "Older workers suffer most as industry carries out reorganization". In The Toronto Star on August 30, 1988 there was an editorial entitled: "Treat older workers with more respect", and the article comments on the problems to which I have referred.
That is the situation that prevailed during the last few years while the Government did nothing. We have a rapidly developing economy with many structural changes, with great developments, and technological change which require updating and restructuring. Sometimes this is very difficult for older workers. When plants are closed due to mergers, restructuring, or rationalization and large segments of the workforce are laid off, it has been found that those situations impact more on older workers than on younger workers. For some older workers it is difficult to adjust and retrain.
Some of the reports define older workers and the problems relating to older workers to be that group between 45 and 65. Other reports define older workers as being over 50, and other reports define them as being over 55. Let's be frank, people in that age group, whether it is from 45 or 50 are people who still have heavy responsibilities. Many of them have children in

May 17, 1989
Labour
university with very high expenses. Many of them are still paying off mortgages. They cannot afford to be without income. Most of them would rather go on working. They feel that they have to go on working, and they want to go on working, but they cannot find work. There are others who are burned out and need enough help to see them through until they are 65 and collect pensions and Old Age Security.
The situation which impacts on older workers is a serious one. Nothing was done, despite many reports, for more than three years. However, worse still, while this situation was in existence and nothing was being done, the Government was taking action that was making it even worse for those workers. There have been cuts in unemployment insurance. We spent half of the last Parliament condemning the Government for cutting unemployment insurance for people who retired early. There were people in the Armed Forces, in the RCMP, and in many segments of Canadian life who were laid off early, most often against their will, who had paid into the Unemployment Insurance Program and finally the Government changed the rules in the middle of the game and cut those people off.
That action on behalf of the Government was responsible for the defeat of several government Members in the last election. The former Minister of Employment and Immigration, the former Member from Kingston, was the one who introduced the program for cutting unemployment insurance for older workers and people who had forced early retirement. She comes from a city where there are many retired military personnel, personnel from the Correctional Service, and many people who have retired early for many reasons.
Yet, despite those reports which stated that there was a crisis and that something should be done, the Government was going in the other direction and cutting unemployment insurance. From 1984 to 1988 the Government cut training and retraining programs by 32 per cent. The Government cut those programs from $2.2 billion in 1984 to $1.5 billion this year. It increased taxes. In this recent Budget the Government is clawing back Old Age Security, reducing Old Age Security, reducing unemployment insurance coverage, and cutting back on regional development and other things that would help workers who are seeking employment. The Government is finally taking action but the program is inadequate.
The Bill provides that special assistance for older workers should go to workers 55 and over, up to the age 65. I would like to hear evidence before the legislative committee whether the age should be 50 years or even 45 to qualify for this special assistance in view of the reports I have received. One has to consider whether the problems of older workers start earlier than 55, as some of the reports indicate.
Clause 5(1) states that subject to the approval of the Governor in Council the Minister may enter into agreements to provide periodic assistance to older workers who are permanently laid off.
The assistance provided under this legislation is not compulsory or automatic for older workers who lose their work permanently. It is subject to the discretion of the Minister, who may enter into agreements.
I and many others have suggested that when certain conditions prevail in the market-place of a certain community and workers are permanently unemployed, it should trigger an assistance program that is not left to the discretion of the Minister. Unemployment insurance is not subject to the discretion of the Minister. If one is laid off due to conditions beyond one's control, unemployment insurance is paid automatically.
According to this Bill, the Minister may enter into agreements to provide for this assistance. The legislation refers to the purpose of making provision for periodic income assistance payments to older workers permanently laid off. It does nor define "periodic income assistance payments". We are led to believe that this assistance could be up to $1,100 a month, but there is no authoritative statement on that. It is left to the discretion of the Minister and the Government so that we do not really know what range of assistance will be available for these workers.
The Bill goes on to state that this assistance will only go to those workers who lose their work as a result of a permanent reduction in the work-force. Again, who interprets what is a permanent reduction in the workforce? Sometimes it is very difficult to determine whether a lay-off or a reduction will be permanent. It could go on for months or even years and someone might consider that it is not permanent. That must be clarified. There must be a definition that will oblige the Government to
May 17, 1989

enter into assistance programs if certain conditions prevail.
This Bill is a move in the right direction. It is too little, too late, but we will support it at this stage so that it will be sent to committee where it can be studied by either the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration or by a legislative committee. We want to hear testimony on the Bill. We want to hear from experts who know something about the subject.
We believe that the Government should have had a more comprehensive approach to the problems of older workers, as suggested in the many reports to which I have referred.
Workers over the age of 50 have a lot to offer. They have a lot of skills and a lot of experience. They have stability. Many of them want to continue to work but when they are laid off from a job they have had for 20 or 30 years, they need counselling, retraining and they need placement assistance. Very often they want to phase down their work from full time into part-time work. This Bill does nothing about that.
While the Bill addresses somewhat the needs of those who have to retire or want to retire because they are burned out, we believe it is not enough.
In conclusion, this is another example of the Government's approach to these matters, and another example of its broken promises. It took more than three years, February, 1986, to May, 1989, to bring in this legislation. It is another example of its laissez-faire approach to a problem that requires serious attention and a comprehensive solution. We intend to study this legislation very closely when it gets to committee.

Mr. Speaker, I want to commend my colleague for an excellent evaluation of the Bill.
Let me bring to his attention a situation in my riding, in relation to the lay-off at Lundy Steel in the town of Dunnville.
I have received letters from older workers, and I want to read part of a letter from a worker who is 58 years old. He worked there for 31 years. He said: "I have supported the community, paid taxes, paid into UIC, paid union dues all these years and now it seems there is no aid for me. The company has never been easy to negotiate with for a contract, and consequently the monthly pension we have in this area is $480".
Labour
He goes on to say that he understands that some provinces have POWAs and he keeps hearing about CSTEC programs, but these are for younger people.
He asked what programs are available for older workers in Ontario, specifically in the Dunnville area. I have met with people from Lundy Steel. Quite frankly, I have been unable to find any programs that are presently available to them. In fact, when I read this Bill I cannot see anything that states the people in Dunnville, Ontario, will be covered by this legislation.
Specifically, it states that the Minister may enter into agreements with provincial Governments. It would seem to me that if the Minister was serious about providing a program for older workers he would bring in a program that is mandatory across the board.
Why does the Member think the Government would go through this charade? Why does he believe it would provide a program that will do nothing to help the people of Lundy Steel in Dunnville, because the Government has not yet negotiated a program with the Ontario Government?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague is absolutely correct that there is no assurance that the community he referred to will be helped by the Bill. According to the Bill, the Minister may enter into agreements with provincial Governments, employer organizations or employee organizations or financial institutions in different parts of the country, but it is very discretionary. There is no assurance that the people with the most serious problems will be cared for, and we do not even know to what level. The Bill leaves a lot up in the air.
The budget announced so far for the program is $125 million for approximately five years. That means approximately $25 million a year is to be spread to ten provinces and two Territories.
Furthermore, while eight provinces have said they intend to participate in the program, only three have signed agreements. I believe the Hon. Member's province so far has not gone into this program at all.
These are the matters about which we are very concerned. This looks like a good program on paper, but when one reads the Bill one does not see very much. We support the Bill at this stage, so that it can go to committee where we can hear experts on the Bill and perhaps people from communities like Dunnville, who can tell us about a real life experience with older worker

unemployment. We can hear from those people and get some suggestions about how we can improve the Bill.
It is my hope that the committee which deals with the Bill will amend it to make it better, and send it back to the House so we can support it with greater enthusiasm.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in today's debate on Bill C-8, an Act to amend the Department of Labour Act. It basically provides older workers adjustment assistance.
I rise in this debate as a Member who represents a number of citizens who should have been the recipients of such programs and on behalf of others who may have to rely on them in the future, assuming my Province of Ontario and the federal Government reach an agreement. I am thinking of the people of Atikokan, a small former mining community of about 6,000. In 1979, Atikokan's whole industry was shut down and 1,100 men were thrown out of work with no other opportunities within that community for them to use their skills. Many of those people, particularly those in the 45 to 65 year old age group were for a number of reasons unable to replace their employment.
These men were open-pit miners. The bodies of many of them, particularly of the older men, had been abused by the kind of work they did and the equipment they operated. While they were able to continue their employment with the companies for which they worked, either Steep Rock or Caland, their skills were not marketable. No one wanted to knowingly acquire the workers' compensation nightmares of the previous employers. Neither would they choose a man of 50 if a man of 25 is available.
Second, these men lived in a community in which they had lived for 25 or more years. They had brought up families and owned homes in this community. It would have been a great expense for them to relocate should they have found employment elsewhere. They got no help from the federal Government of the day.
A co-ordinating committee was set up and civil servants came to talk to these people. Studies were done, but the bottom line was that they got no help.
Even today, there are still men younger than 65 who have no gainful employment. The community in which they live held no other opportunities for them. They could not move to underground mines within the northwest because that required different skills. There were attempts made to give them retraining opportunities, but by and large, all society did was raise their level of expectations only to pull the rug out from underneath them.
These people live in a community that has a current unemployment rate of 25 per cent. An employment study was done of half the community two years ago. Ironically, it is only in the smaller communities that one can do a really good sampling to get a sense of unemployment levels. This study showed that one out of every two residents of Atikokan who was available or willing to work held employment during that year. A large percentage of the unemployed were in the older worker category.
These people could be helped by this legislation if they were to be laid off today. However, they will not be helped because it happened too long ago. We have to learn from that experience.
All of us who come from resource-based communities know that a mine begins to die the day the first shovel is put in the ground. The resources are finite, unlike the forestry sector which at least in theory is renewable, although the federal Government and many provincial Governments have not done what they should have done to protect those resources.
In the forestry based communities, we will also see massive lay-offs because the industry has been cutting trees farther and farther away from the pulp and paper mills or sawmills. There will come a point when lay-offs will have to be made, and we are seeing that point in northwestern Ontario these days. It is partly because of what I was talking about, the greater distance between the mill and the harvesting area. Therefore the cost of production goes up. As well, it is as a result of the policies of the Government which has given in to the United States on the softwood lumber dispute. We are the victims of that, the communities that are losing employment. The people of these communities will have to rely on the $1,100 a month maximum allowable under this program to replace decent union wages of $15 to $20 per hour, wages that could provide a man and a woman
May 17, 1989

Labour
with the income to sustain a family in a northern community. Unfortunately, we will need a lot of access to this program.
I read in some of the documents I have that at the most, 5,000 people will be served by this program. Without much difficulty, I could find 5,000 men and women in northwestern Ontario who would need this program. Their employment will be taken away from them because of economic conditions, because of the high dollar and because of their inability to compete with the Americans or on the world market. They will lose their jobs because of government policy, because of a shortage of wood fibre or because the mineral body has run out. This may not happen tomorrow. It might not happen for 10, 15 or 20 years, but the great Hemlo mine will disappear and with it the boom of Marathon and surrounding communities. Those people will also be in need of a program. By the time that ore body runs out, those workers will be eligible for the Older Worker Adjustment Program.
I can find those 5,000 workers today just in northwestern Ontario. I can go to my own community of Thunder Bay and look at those who work in the grain industry in which in excess of 1,200 men and women were laid off. Add to that the people who work the boats on the Great Lakes and the people who work in the ports downstream from Thunder Bay. Many of them are in that particular age group. Will they be helped by this program? I am not so sure. It does not deal with cyclical lay-offs. It does not deal with the reality of a number of grain-handlers in Thunder Bay who have not worked enough weeks in the last two or three years to allow them to continue to receive unemployment insurance benefits. The bureaucrats will say that they cannot be eligible for this program because they are not permanently laid off. The reality is that there will be fewer and fewer permanent employees working in those elevators from here on in.
Yes, there is a seniority provision that pretty well guarantees that those who have worked there long enough will retain their jobs, although we are seeing people with 15 and 20 years seniority being laid off now. Yes, they will get called back, but there are others in the community who will not be called back, and that is also something with which we have to deal.
The Government of Canada has known the needs of older workers for a number of years. I am sure that in opposition the Conservatives demanded programs of the Liberals to provide protection for older workers. I know we did, because we recognized that on one hand we had an ageing population. On the other hand we recognized the unfortunate realities of how employers view older men and women as being less of a positive investment than a younger worker. We recognized that employers did not look at the quality that they would be getting. Quite frankly, many of these older workers have a lot to contribute, have a lot of knowledge and have a lot of experience.
In societies of days gone past we would look to those older workers for leadership-not just those below 65 but those well above 65-in terms of where we should be going from here, our teachers. Today we tend to put them on the slag heap and leave them to rot.
In addition to dealing with the specific lay-off problems, what we as a society should be doing is making it possible for all our people to afford to live in today's society. As part of that we should make sure that more and more people can afford to retire earlier than they do today. Yes, we have a modest step forward with the changes to the Canada Pension Plan providing for the early out option. Some people are taking advantage of it. I know that between 1984 and 1988 a number of people in the riding of Thunder Bay-Atikokan, and in fact northwestern Ontario, took advantage of it. That did help. That was a form of older worker adjustment.
People of Atikokan took advantage of it. Those who had been laid off and could find no other work were able to get some level of income. I think that we as a society have to work for the day when people can afford to leave the workforce at 55 or at 60 so that in turn those employment opportunities are available for our younger people. We must ensure that they have the income level that is appropriate for their needs and allows them to continue on as full participants in society in a volunteer capacity or whatever capacity they choose.
I do not want to go on much longer. I know that my other colleagues want to participate today. I believe it is important that we do provide these services. It is also important that we provide even more than what we are providing in this legislation. I would encourage if not demand the Province of Ontario and the Government of

I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your attention. I look forward with interest to the remarks of my colleagues and completion of all studies of this Bill.
